title: Blame
author: Tom Geraghty
summary: Tom Geraghty takes on the misconception that psychological safety means a blameless culture. He argues blame is sometimes appropriate, for example for deliberate harm, and that clear standards help foster safety. He defines blame as accountability without context and coins blametropism for our instinctive urge to assign fault to individuals, which is reinforced by the fundamental attribution error, moral luck and incident investigations that conclude the human did it. Because blame presumes intent and most failures in complex systems involve no bad intent, jumping to blame stops the learning that would prevent repeats. Publicly imposed blame also teaches others to hide mistakes. His recommended stance is to be blame-aware rather than blameless: treat errors as information about the system, apply the Local Rationality Principle, and check whether blaming is constructive or merely satisfying.
points: Psychological safety does not require a blameless culture; deliberate harm can warrant blame, and upholding standards makes expectations explicit.
Blametropism is a near-universal instinct to attribute failure to individual character instead of the context and system in which people acted.
Blame is tied to intent, yet in complex systems the person at fault rarely intended harm, so stopping at blame forfeits learning.
Public blame teaches others to hide mistakes and suppress concerns, which damages the team culture it is meant to protect.
The practical alternative is being blame-aware: treat errors as system information and ask whether blame is constructive or only emotionally satisfying.
quotes: It’s a common fallacy that psychological safety means having a “blameless” culture. Just like so many misconceptions around psychological safety, that’s not actually the case.
Blame can be considered “accountability without context“, so a powerful way to address blame is to actively and explicitly consider context.
If we jump to blame, we can easily miss all this nuance and any opportunities to better understand and learn from the multitude of compounding factors.
Instead of fostering learning, this may instead foster resentment and damage confidence in someone’s capability or self-worth.
What’s more, publicly-imposed blame is likely to teach others to hide their mistakes, suppress their concerns, and “keep their head down” lest they suffer the same public humiliation.
A far more constructive and utilitarian approach is to treat errors, mistakes and violations as sources of valuable information about the system.

By recognising our own inherent blametropism – our innate instinct to apportion blame – and becoming blame-aware instead of (maybe naively) attempting to be entirely blameless or blame-free, we can check in with ourselves and others to help determine whether we’re blaming because it’ll make us feel better, or whether it’s actually a constructive thing to do.
